questions.text: Which statement about DFAs and NFAs is TRUE?

options.text: NFAs recognise strictly more languages than DFAs
Every NFA has an equivalent DFA
NFAs are always smaller and faster to simulate

questions.solution: The subset construction converts any NFA to a DFA, so both recognise exactly the regular languages. The DFA may have up to 2<sup>n</sup> states, which is where the cost shows up — not in expressive power.

questions.text: An NFA has 4 states. What is the maximum number of states in the equivalent DFA produced by the subset construction?
questions.solution: Each DFA state is a subset of the NFA's states, so there are at most 2<sup>4</sup> = 16, including the empty set which acts as a dead state.

questions.text: What is the minimum number of states in a DFA over {0, 1} that accepts all strings whose length is divisible by 3?
questions.solution: The only thing to remember is the length modulo 3, which has three possible values. Three states in a cycle, with the state for remainder 0 accepting, suffices — and no fewer, since the three residues are pairwise distinguishable.

questions.text: Which language is regular?
questions.solution: a*b* needs no counting, so it is regular. Option A requires matching counts (context-free but not regular), C requires remembering an arbitrary string, and D needs three matched counts (not even context-free).

questions.text: Which machine corresponds to context-free languages in the Chomsky hierarchy?
questions.solution: The hierarchy pairs regular with finite automata, context-free with pushdown automata, context-sensitive with linear bounded automata, and recursively enumerable with Turing machines. The stack is exactly what lets a PDA match nested structure.

questions.text: Which closure properties hold for regular languages?
questions.solution: Regular languages are closed under all of these — union and star by construction on NFAs, complement by swapping accepting states of a complete DFA, and intersection via the product construction or De Morgan. Context-free languages, by contrast, are not closed under intersection or complement.

questions.text: The halting problem is:

options.text: Neither recursively enumerable nor co-recursively enumerable

questions.solution: You can semi-decide halting by simulating the machine: if it halts you will see it. What you cannot do is conclude non-halting in finite time, so the language is recursively enumerable but not recursive. Its complement is not even RE.

questions.text: Which problems are undecidable?

options.text: Whether a given DFA accepts the empty language
Whether two context-free grammars generate the same language
Whether a Turing machine halts on a given input
Whether a given CFG generates any string at all

questions.solution: DFA emptiness is decidable by reachability, and CFG emptiness is decidable by checking whether the start symbol is generating. CFG equivalence and the halting problem are both undecidable — CFG equivalence reduces from the Post Correspondence Problem.

questions.text: The pumping lemma for regular languages is used to prove that a language is:
questions.solution: The lemma states a property every regular language must have, so it can only be used negatively: show the property fails and the language cannot be regular. Satisfying the lemma does not prove regularity — the converse does not hold.

questions.text: What is the key difference between a Mealy machine and a Moore machine?

options.text: Mealy output depends on state and input; Moore output depends only on state
Mealy machines have no final states
Moore machines cannot be converted to Mealy machines

questions.solution: A Moore machine labels outputs on states; a Mealy machine labels them on transitions, so its output can react within the same clock cycle. The two are inter-convertible, with a Moore machine needing at most one extra state.

questions.text: Which compiler phase is most directly built on finite automata?
questions.solution: Tokens are described by regular expressions, which compile to finite automata — that is exactly what a lexer is. Syntax analysis needs the extra power of a pushdown automaton because grammars nest.

questions.text: A grammar is ambiguous if:

options.text: Some string has more than one distinct parse tree
It has more than one non-terminal

questions.solution: Ambiguity is about parse trees, not about the shape of the productions. Left recursion is a separate problem that breaks top-down parsers but does not by itself imply ambiguity. Some context-free languages are inherently ambiguous — no unambiguous grammar exists for them.

questions.text: What is the minimum number of states in a DFA over {a, b} that accepts exactly those strings ending in ab?
questions.solution: The machine only needs to know how much of ab it has just seen: nothing useful, a trailing a, or a trailing ab. Three states, with the last accepting. Fewer is impossible because those three situations are pairwise distinguishable — b, b and ε separate them.

questions.text: What is the minimum number of states in a DFA over {0, 1} that accepts binary strings whose value is divisible by 3, reading most significant bit first?
questions.solution: Track the value modulo 3, which has three possible remainders. Reading a bit b takes remainder r to (2r + b) mod 3, and the state for remainder 0 accepts. The three residues are pairwise distinguishable, so three states is also the minimum.

questions.text: Which language cannot be accepted by any finite automaton?

options.text: Strings over {a, b} containing an even number of a's

questions.solution: Matching the counts of a and b requires remembering n, which is unbounded, and a finite automaton has only finitely many states. The pumping lemma makes this precise. The others need only bounded information.

questions.text: Which statements about a deterministic finite automaton are TRUE?

options.text: It has exactly one transition per state per input symbol
It may have more than one accepting state
It has exactly one start state

questions.solution: Determinism means the next state is fully decided by the current state and input symbol, so epsilon transitions are not allowed — those belong to NFAs. Any number of accepting states is fine, but there is always exactly one start state.

questions.text: On what principle does DFA minimisation rest?

options.text: Merging states that cannot be distinguished by any input string
Converting the DFA to an NFA first

questions.solution: Two states are equivalent when no string leads one to acceptance and the other to rejection. Merging every such class gives the unique minimal DFA, a result known as the Myhill-Nerode theorem. Partition refinement computes it.

questions.text: Context-free grammars are which type in the Chomsky hierarchy?
questions.solution: Type 0 is unrestricted, type 1 context-sensitive, type 2 context-free and type 3 regular. The numbering runs from most to least general, so every type 3 grammar is also type 2.

questions.text: Why is left recursion a problem?

options.text: It makes a top-down parser recurse forever without consuming input
It prevents the grammar from being converted to Chomsky normal form

questions.solution: A rule such as A → Aα leads a recursive descent parser to call A again with the same input position, so it never terminates. Bottom-up parsers handle left recursion without difficulty. Left recursion and ambiguity are separate issues — a grammar can have either without the other.

questions.text: A grammar is in Chomsky normal form when every production has the form:
questions.solution: Two non-terminals or a single terminal on the right, plus S → ε if the empty string is in the language. Option B is right-linear form, which characterises regular grammars. CNF is what makes the CYK parsing algorithm work.

questions.text: Which grammar generates { a<sup>n</sup>b<sup>n</sup> | n ≥ 0 }?
questions.solution: Each application adds one a on the left and one b on the right, keeping the counts equal and the a's all before the b's. Option A generates every string over {a, b}, and option C generates a*b.

questions.text: Under which operations are context-free languages closed?
questions.solution: Union, concatenation and star can all be built directly by combining grammars. Intersection fails: a<sup>n</sup>b<sup>n</sup>c<sup>m</sup> and a<sup>m</sup>b<sup>n</sup>c<sup>n</sup> are both context-free but their intersection a<sup>n</sup>b<sup>n</sup>c<sup>n</sup> is not. Complement fails too, since closure under complement plus union would give intersection.

questions.text: A non-terminal in a context-free grammar is useless when:

options.text: it appears on the right of no production
it derives no terminal string, or is unreachable from the start symbol
it appears in more than one production

questions.solution: Both failures make a symbol useless: one that generates no terminal string can never finish a derivation, and one the start symbol cannot reach can never begin one. Removing them changes nothing about the language, and the order matters — eliminate non-generating symbols first, then unreachable ones.
